# Part 1

## 1.1 Introduction

and the response variable 'price-thousands'. The goal is to fit and diagnose a linear model
that explains the price of houses based on the three predictors using matrix computation.

# Part 2

``` {python}
predictors = df[["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]].to_numpy()
y = df["price_thousands"].to_numpy()
```

### Standardize the Predictors

``` {python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (predictors- means) / sds
```

Mean across the predictors = `{python} print(Z.mean(axis=0))`
Standard deviation across the predictors: `{python} print(Z.std(axis=0))`

### Construct the Design matrix

``` {python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])
```

The 'predictors' array (an array containing the values of each of the three explanatory variables
for each observation) is 3-dimensional with 130 elements (`{python} predictors.shape`).

``` {python}
predictors.shape
```

The 'Z' array (an array containing the Z-scores of each explanatory variable for each observation)
also is 3-dimensional with 130 elements (`{python} Z.shape`).

``` {python}
Z.shape
```

The 'X' array (an array that acts as the design matrix for the computations) is 4-dimensional
with 130 elements (`{python} X.shape`). The extra dimension only contains 1s.

``` {python}
X.shape
```

The 'y' array (an array with the response values (price in thousands) for each observation) is
1-dimensional with 130 elements (`{python} y.shape`).

``` {python}
y.shape
```

The matrix rank of X is `{python} print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`.

``` {python}
np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
```

There are three predictors excluding the intercept. This is clear when looking at the number of
dimensions of 'predictors'.

``` {python}
predictors.shape
```

## Written Response

X and y must have compatable shapes because they both represent the observed variable values
(response variable values in y and predictor variable values in X) as elements, so the number of
observations (number of elements) must match between X and y. The intercept column is necessary
in X because X will be multiplied (as a matrix) by the beta matrix which includes the intercept
beta (beta0). Standardizing the predictors puts all the predictors on a common scale without
altering their relationship to the response or their distribution. Broadcasting allows the code
to complete element-wise subtraction of the mean from the predictor values (predictor - mean) and
division of the standard deviation (/ sds) in order to complete the same calculations without a
loop.

# Part 3

### Fit the Model

``` {python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond = None)
```

Estimated Coefficients:
Intercept coefficient = `{python} print(beta_hat[0])`
size_sqft coefficient = `{python} print(beta_hat[1])`
bedrooms coefficient = `{python} print(beta_hat[2])`
age_years coefficient = `{python} print(beta_hat[3])`

size_sqft has the largest absolute value coefficient (`{python} print(beta_hat[1])`).

### Calculate Fitted Values and Residuals

``` {python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y- fitted
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))
```

The mean of the residuals is `{python} print(residuals.mean())`, and the RMSE is `{python} print(rmse)`.

## Written Response

X @ beta_hat represents the predicted outcome for observation based on the estimated beta values
and the observation's predictor values. The residual mean should be near zero when an intercept is
present because the difference between the observed response values and the predicted response
values is close to zero when the predictions are accurate. RMSE summarizes how far a model’s
predictions are from the actual observed response values, on average. X * beta_hat uses element-wise
multiplication while X @ beta_hat uses matrix multiplication.

# Part 4

## QR Decomposition

``` {python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
```

Q has 4 dimensions with 130 elements (`{python} Q.shape`) while R has 4 dimensions with 4
elements (`{python} R.shape`).

Multiplying Q and R results in the design matrix (X), and the dimensions of Q are orthogonal.

``` {python}
np.allclose(Q @ R, X)
```

``` {python}
np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1]))
```

## SVD

``` {python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
```

U is 4-dimensional with 130 elements (`{python} U.shape`), s is 1-dimentional with 4 elements
(`{python} s.shape`), and Vt is 4-dimensional with 4 elements (`{python} Vt.shape`).

The singular values are `{python} print(s[0].round(2))`, `{python} print(s[1].round(2))`,
`{python} print(s[2].round(2))`, and `{python} print(s[3].round(2))`.

``` {python}
X_reconstructed = (U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt)
```

The reconstructed design matrix (reconstructed X) is similar to the original design matrix (X)
that was created in Part 2.

``` {python}
np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X)
```

## Rank and Conditioning

The rank of the design matrix (X) is `{python} print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`. The largest
singular value is about `{python} print(np.linalg.cond(X).round(2))` times the smallest which
means that the design matrix (X) is well conditioned.

``` {python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])
```

The largest singular value of the raw design matrix (raw X) is about
`{python} print(np.linalg.cond(X_raw).round(2))` times the smallest which means that the raw
design matric (raw X) is not well conditioned.

## Written Response

Q @ R ≈ X verifies that Q and R really are a decomposition of X, and Q.T @ Q ≈ I verifies that
the dimensions of Q are orthogonal. Each singular value measures how much the design matrix (X)
stretched the input in one direction. A large condition number suggests that the design matrix is
not well conditioned because X stretches by a different amount in each direction. The condition
number did change after standardization. Mismatched measurement scales can inflate the raw
condition number because singular values are based on each column/dimension's units. Because the
condition number of the standardized design matrix was low
(`{python} print(np.linalg.cond(X).round(2))`), it does not show evidence of severe redundancy
among predictors.
